Think–Pair–Share · What is inside a phone?

  3. Share: improve your answer using your partner’s idea.

Extension (HPGE) · Case evidence

E-waste council · Where should a phone go?

A council is planning a school e-waste collection. The team must recover useful materials safely. Do not dismantle devices or batteries.

Phone partEvidenceConstraint
WiringCopper conducts wellRecover through approved recycling
CasingAluminium is light for its strengthSeparate through authorised processing
BatteryLithium-containing electrode materials support rechargeable energy storageDamaged batteries need specialist handling

Start: Act as a recycler or school safety adviser. Recommend two collection priorities.

Marsden High School · Science 2027L01 · 19
Extension (HPGE) · Analyse, evaluate, create

Your challenge · E-waste council

  1. Act as a recycler or school safety adviser. Recommend two collection priorities.
  2. Use two pieces of evidence and challenge the claim 'a phone is made of one element'.
  3. Agree on a safe collection rule and identify one fact still needed.

Check your work: A reasoned recommendation, safe handling, evidence and an unanswered question.

Reveal possible reasoning / teacher guide
Prioritise approved collection of whole devices and specialist battery handling. Copper and aluminium are useful but the phone contains many materials; battery compounds are not loose lithium metal. Ask the authorised recycler what it accepts.

Frayer model · Metal

Use copper, aluminium, sulfur and silicon as your examples to test the meaning of metal.

Extension (HPGE) · Analyse, evaluate, create

Your challenge · Classification panel

  1. Challenge the rule 'all conductors are metals' using the evidence.
  2. Propose a classification rule that uses more than one property; classify each material.
  3. Defend why silicon may be useful in electronics and state a limitation of the rule.

Core learning · practise, check, improve

Predict–Observe–Explain · Will the lamp light?

A teacher-approved low-voltage circuit tests copper and sulfur samples. Predict before seeing the results.

  1. Predict which solid will complete the circuit and why.
  2. Observe the teacher’s demonstration or use the supplied results: copper lights the lamp; sulfur does not.
  3. Explain whether the result supports your prediction and revise it if necessary.

Check your work: Distinguish a prediction from an observation, and link the result to conductivity.

Show an example after discussion
I predicted copper would conduct. The lamp lit with copper, supporting my prediction. The lamp did not light with sulfur.

Independent practice

You do · Independent question

Marsden High School · Science 2027L03 · 16
Practical / application

Run the property test

1. Teacher checks goggles, approved samples and low-voltage circuit. 2. Observe appearance. 3. Test electrical conductivity. 4. Apply agreed scratch-test method/rating. 5. Record and compare. No hazardous samples.

SampleAppearanceConducts?Scratch rating (1–5)Likely class
A
B
C
Teacher guide

Actual results vary. Compare under consistent conditions; a shiny conducting sample is likely metallic. Record uncertain observations.

Extension (HPGE) · Case evidence

Lab review board · Are the results trustworthy?

Three groups tested the same known copper sample with low-voltage equipment. The lamp results are fictional.

GroupTrial 1Trial 2Trial 3
ALightsLightsLights
BOffLightsOff
CLightsLightsLights

Start: Rank the strength of the evidence from the three groups and justify your ranking.

Marsden High School · Science 2027L03 · 19
Extension (HPGE) · Analyse, evaluate, create

Your challenge · Lab review board

  1. Rank the strength of the evidence from the three groups and justify your ranking.
  2. Propose two possible reasons for the inconsistent group B results.
  3. Design a repeat-test plan with a known conductor and a clear recording rule.

Check your work: Recognise inconsistent evidence; improve the method without deleting inconvenient results.

Reveal possible reasoning / teacher guide
A and C have consistent results; B is uncertain. Loose clips or a flat battery could explain the inconsistency. Check the circuit using a known conductor, use consistent contacts, repeat and keep all results.

Claim–Evidence–Reasoning · Choose a wire

Copper conducts electricity and can be drawn into wire. Rubber is a poor conductor.

  3. Reasoning: link that property to the function. Swap answers and improve the because-clause.

Check your work: A claim, a specific property and a logical link to the use.

Show an example after discussion

Marsden High School · Science 2027L09 · 09
READ literacy task

READ · Atomic models (1 of 2)

Scientists use models to represent objects that are too small to see directly. An atomic model is not a photograph of an atom. It is a representation that helps explain observations.

In the early nineteenth century, John Dalton described matter as made of tiny atoms. His model treated atoms as solid particles. Later, experiments with cathode rays provided evidence for negatively charged electrons. J. J. Thomson proposed a model in which electrons were embedded in positively charged matter.

Marsden High School · Science 2027L09 · 10
READ literacy task

READ · Atomic models (2 of 2)

In the early twentieth century, Ernest Rutherford and colleagues studied how positively charged particles travelled towards thin gold foil. Most passed through, but a small number were deflected through large angles. This evidence suggested that most of the atom was empty space, with much of its mass and positive charge concentrated in a small nucleus.

Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons could occupy particular energy levels. This helped explain the pattern of spectral lines from hydrogen. The simple shell diagrams used in school are based on this idea, but do not show the exact motion or position of electrons.

Each model was useful in its time. When new evidence challenged an earlier model, scientists developed a better representation. Modern atomic models are more detailed, and scientists continue to test explanations against evidence.

Your challenge · Prediction audit

The groups have opposite trends. Rb is generally more reactive than K; I is generally less reactive than Br. Specific reactions and conditions require reliable reference data.

Extension (HPGE) · Case evidence

Historical science debate · Leave a gap or fill it?

Mendeleev left gaps and predicted missing elements; Moseley later established atomic-number ordering. The table below is a fictional pattern model, not historical measurements.

PositionObserved / predicted patternStatus
1Property score 2Known
2Property score 4Known
3Property score about 6Missing
4Property score 8Known

Start: Debate whether to leave position 3 empty or force a known element into it.

Marsden High School · Science 2027L17 · 19
Extension (HPGE) · Analyse, evaluate, create

Your challenge · Historical science debate

  1. Debate whether to leave position 3 empty or force a known element into it.
  2. Predict what evidence a later discovery would need to match to support the gap.
  3. Explain why changing from mass-based to atomic-number ordering is an example of scientific refinement.

Check your work: Make a testable prediction, defend a choice and distinguish a pattern from proof.

Reveal possible reasoning / teacher guide
A gap preserves the pattern and predicts a score near 6. A later matching observation supports but does not prove the organisation. Atomic-number evidence improved the ordering.
